Transcript: Let’s discuss asymmetric information in labor markets—a concept that’s vital for understanding how wages and hiring decisions are made. Why does this matter? Well, when employers and employees have different levels of information, it can lead to inefficiencies and even market failures, affecting not just individuals but the broader economy as well. The classic example of asymmetric information is the “lemons problem,” first described by economist George Akerlof. In the used car market, sellers typically know much more about the quality of their cars than buyers do, which can drive down prices and push high-quality cars out of the market. The interesting thing here is that a similar dynamic plays out in labor markets: job applicants know more about their skills, work ethic, and reliability than potential employers. For example, consider a company trying to fill a technical position. The employer can’t directly observe a candidate’s coding ability or problem-solving skills during the initial hiring process. What researchers have found is that, in these situations, firms often rely on educational credentials or previous job titles as proxies for actual skill. But actually—let me clarify—credentials aren’t always a perfect signal.

Some highly skilled workers might lack formal degrees due to financial or personal reasons, while others with impressive diplomas may not perform as well on the job as their resumes suggest. There’s also the issue of “credential inflation,” where jobs require higher and higher degrees, not necessarily because the work is more complex, but because employers are searching for any reliable signal of ability. Another consequence of asymmetric information is adverse selection. Employers, unsure about the true ability of applicants, may offer lower starting wages to protect themselves from hiring unproductive workers. A dozen of the plays printed under one name in 1623 have at various times been given a collaborator, and for most of the twentieth century the case rested on parallels: a phrase in a disputed scene that turns up again in a play securely assigned to somebody else, and nowhere in between.

A parallel counts for something only if the searching behind it was exhaustive, and the searchable corpus of the period is uneven, some genres transcribed in full and others hardly at all. The lists were also compiled by readers who already suspected where the joins lay, and a reader looking for a phrase in a particular scene finds phrases in that scene.

Vickers puts the objection at the negative check. A collocation offered as unique to two authors has to be run against the whole corpus before it is called unique, and in a great many published attributions that search was never carried out; on his account the tally of shared rarities is a tally of what one investigator happened to notice.

One school treats the question as badly formed. A playhouse text was cut, patched and revised by whoever was to hand, so the search for a second author imposes a category the theatre never used.

The grammatical habits that survive that filter are of another kind: whether a writer reaches for the older third-person ending or the newer one, which relative pronoun he uses for a person, how often the possessive is built with an apostrophe rather than with a following preposition.
